Detection that depends on abundance: the Royle-Nichols model

Source: vignettes/royle-nichols.Rmd
royle-nichols.Rmd

In fp_occu(), the probability of detecting the species at an occupied site is the same function of covariates at every site. In reality, a site with many calling individuals is detected more often than a site with one. Variation in detection among sites then has two possible sources: abundance, and everything else (distance to the recorder, background noise, vegetation). fp_occu() with random_det = TRUE captures the sum of both, but cannot tell them apart.

fp_occu_rn() fits the model of Royle and Nichols (2003), in which detection depends on abundance, with the false positives and verification of fp_occu(). A site effect on the per-individual detection rate then measures the variation in detection that abundance does not explain. This article describes the model, shows how to fit and check it, and reports the simulations that show what it can and cannot recover. The fitting code is shown but not run when the article is built.

The model

The number of individuals at site i is N_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i), with \log \lambda_i = X_i \beta + v_i. The site is occupied when N_i > 0, so the occupancy probability is \psi_i = 1 - e^{-\lambda_i}. Each individual is detected on an occasion with probability r, and the automated method detects at least one with probability 1 - (1 - r_{ik})^{N_i}, where \mathrm{logit}(r_{ik}) = Z_{ik} \alpha + d_i. False positives occur on every automated occasion with probability p_{10}, also at occupied sites. An occasion is a detection when either a true or a false observation occurs: \Pr(y_{ik} = 1 \mid N_i) = 1 - (1 - r_{ik})^{N_i} (1 - p_{10,i}). A verified occasion has no false positives and is a detection with probability 1 - (1 - r^{v})^{N_i}. The abundance N_i is summed out of the likelihood over 0 to n_max.

The two site effects are the point of the model:

  • v_i, with standard deviation sd_abund_site (random_abund = TRUE), is variation in abundance beyond the covariates of occ.
  • d_i, with standard deviation sd_det_site (random_det = TRUE), is variation in the per-individual detection rate.

Both raise the variance of detections among occupied sites. They differ in what else they predict. Abundance also changes the share of occupied sites and the detection by the verified method. A detection effect changes only the automated detections. Verified or confirmed occasions are therefore what separates the two.

There are two ways to provide that information:

  • Verified occasions: detections by an independent method without false positives, at some sites (the verified table of fp_data()).
  • Confirmed occasions: automated occasions whose detections were reviewed and split into true and false observations (the confirmed argument of fp_data(), the observation-confirmation design of Chambert et al. 2015). A fully annotated survey confirms every occasion.

Unlike fp_occu(), the false-positive intercept is not tied to the detection intercept by a gap. Detection at an occupied site always exceeds p_{10}, so the labels of true and false detections cannot switch.

Fitting and checking

simulate_fp_rn() generates data from the model. Here 100 sites with 15 automated occasions each, verified occasions at 30% of the sites, and a site effect on detection:

s <- simulate_fp_rn(nsite = 100, nocc = 15, psi = 0.6, b1 = 0.5, r = 0.3,
                    p10 = 0.05, sigma_r = 1, sigma_lam = 0.5,
                    frac_verified = 0.3, nver = 3, seed = 1)

The fit with both site effects:

m <- fp_occu_rn(s$data, occ = ~ x, random_det = TRUE, random_abund = TRUE,
                n_max = 25, iter_warmup = 1500,
                iter_sampling = 1500, seed = 1)
m

Three settings matter more than in fp_occu():

  • n_max must be large enough that the Poisson mass above it is negligible at every site. The fit warns when it is not, from the derived quantity p_above_nmax. The cost of the fit grows with n_max.
  • The default adapt_delta is 0.99, above the 0.95 of fp_occu(). The site effects create funnels, and at 0.95 divergences appeared in most designs of the simulations below.
  • With many sites, the standard deviations of the site effects mix slowly. At 100 sites, 1000 + 1000 iterations left a largest R-hat of 1.01-1.03 in half or more of the simulated fits. Longer chains are the remedy.

Before the estimates, check convergence (R-hat, bulk ESS and divergences in m$diagnostics) and the fit to the data:

fp_ppc(m)                        # automated detections per site
fp_ppc(m, method = "verified")   # verified detections per site

fp_sites() gives, for each site, the posterior probability that it is occupied and its expected abundance given its data:

head(fp_sites(m))   # occupied, abundance, abundance_lower, abundance_upper, ...

loo() estimates the leave-one-site-out predictive density, with the site effects integrated out of each site’s likelihood. Without that integration most sites get high Pareto k. The comparison of interest is usually a model with and without the detection effect:

m0 <- update(m, random_det = FALSE)
fp_loo_weights(with_det = m, without_det = m0)

Calibration

Simulation-based calibration (Talts et al. 2018) checks that the program fits the model the simulator generates. Parameters are drawn from the priors, data are simulated from them, and the rank of each true value among the posterior draws should be uniform. Two designs, 500 datasets each, had 50 sites and 10 occasions: design A confirmed every occasion and had no verified data, and design B confirmed 20% of the occasions and verified 3 occasions at 30% of the sites.

design parameter datasets p (uniformity) mean rank (of 0-100)
A alpha[1] 500 0.280 49.7
A beta[1] 500 0.260 50.6
A beta[2] 500 0.028 45.8
A gamma0 500 0.370 51.7
A sigma_det[1] 500 0.900 49.7
A sigma_lam[1] 500 0.260 49.7
B alpha[1] 500 0.650 50.3
B beta[1] 500 0.830 50.3
B beta[2] 500 0.070 48.6
B delta0 500 0.810 50.4
B gamma0 500 0.850 48.7
B sigma_det[1] 500 0.480 48.0
B sigma_lam[1] 500 0.210 51.1

The ranks are close to uniform. The exception is the slope of log abundance (beta[2]) in design A. Its mean rank is 45.8, about 3 standard errors below 50, and its posterior median lies on average 0.02 above the true value. With 13 tests, a single p-value of 0.03 can arise by chance, and the departure is small. Divergences occurred in 0.2%-0.4% of the fits.

Recovery across designs

The general grid crossed the number of sites (25, 50, 100), occasions (10, 20), the annotation scheme, \sigma_r (0 or 1) and \sigma_\lambda (0 or 0.7), with 100 datasets per cell. The annotation schemes were:

  • verified: 3 verified occasions at 30% of the sites;
  • partial: the same, plus 20% of automated occasions confirmed;
  • full: every occasion confirmed, no verified data.

Other values were fixed (\psi = 0.6, slope 0.5, r = 0.3, p_{10} = 0.05), and the fits used the default priors. A signal is a lower 5% bound of sd_det_site above 0.1. Where \sigma_r = 0, a signal is false. Where \sigma_r = 1, it is power.

Signal for a site effect on detection, with sigma_lambda = 0.7.
sites x occasions power: verified partial full false: verified partial full
25 x 10 51% 46% 55% 11% 7% 12%
25 x 20 51% 59% 70% 6% 8% 8%
50 x 10 68% 69% 70% 7% 5% 12%
50 x 20 79% 84% 80% 7% 7% 9%
100 x 10 83% 86% 84% 7% 11% 11%
100 x 20 93% 93% 94% 5% 6% 1%

Three results stand out:

  • Power grows with the number of sites and occasions, from about half at 25 sites and 10 occasions to above 90% at 100 sites and 20 occasions.
  • Beyond the smallest design, the annotation scheme matters little. Verifying 30% of the sites gave about the same power as confirming every occasion. At 25 sites and 10 occasions without variation in abundance, verified data alone gave less power (41%) than partial confirmation (54%).
  • Variation in abundance raises the false signal only moderately. Without it (\sigma_\lambda = 0) the false signal was 0%-6%; with \sigma_\lambda = 0.7 it was 1%-12%.

The other quantities were well recovered. The 90% intervals covered the true value in 85%-97% of the fits for p_{10}, 81%-99% for r and 85%-99% for \psi. The standard deviation of abundance was weakly identified. When it was 0, its posterior median was 0.24-0.63, the scale of its prior.

Few sites and the prior

A second grid had 21 sites with 11-19 occasions, every occasion confirmed and no verified data, at three occupancy levels. Each dataset was fitted under four priors on sd_det_site: half-Normal with scale 0.5, 1 (the default) and 2, and half-Student-t with 3 degrees of freedom.

21 sites, true sd_det_site = 0, over occupancy and p10.
prior on sd_det_site false signal posterior median
half-Normal(0, 0.5) 0%-1% 0.3-0.39
half-Normal(0, 1) 11%-31% 0.46-0.59
half-Normal(0, 2) 20%-43% 0.55-0.7
half-t(3, 0, 1) 9%-30% 0.44-0.58

With 21 sites the posterior of sd_det_site near 0 follows its prior. The false signal ranges from almost none under the narrowest prior to above 40% under the widest. With few sites, report sd_det_site under more than one prior, through fp_priors(det_site_sd = ). A signal that holds only under wide priors is not evidence of variation in detection.

What the model can and cannot say

  • A large sd_det_site with many sites is good evidence of variation in detection beyond abundance.
  • Evidence for the absence of variation in detection needs a large design. Where \sigma_r = 0, the Savage-Dickey Bayes factor for \sigma_r = 0 exceeded 3 in 0%-3% of the fits at 25 sites and 10 occasions, and in 24%-77% at 100 sites and 20 occasions. Variation in abundance lowers these shares. A small sd_det_site from a small design is not evidence that detection does not vary.
  • sd_abund_site is weakly identified and leans on its prior when the variation in abundance is small.
  • Abundance in this model is a latent quantity that links detection to occupancy. Its scale depends on the assumption that individuals are detected independently with the same r. It should not be read as a count of animals without independent support.

References

Chambert, T., Miller, D. A. W. and Nichols, J. D. (2015). Modeling false positive detections in species occurrence data under different study designs. Ecology, 96, 332-339. https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1

Royle, J. A. and Nichols, J. D. (2003). Estimating abundance from repeated presence-absence data or point counts. Ecology, 84, 777-790. https://doi.org/10.1890/0012-9658(2003)084[0777:EAFRPA]2.0.CO;2

Talts, S., Betancourt, M., Simpson, D., Vehtari, A. and Gelman, A. (2018). Validating Bayesian inference algorithms with simulation-based calibration. arXiv:1804.06788.
